6EXPLANATORY STATEMENT PURSUANT 
TO THE PROVISIONS OF SECTION 102 
OF THE COMPANIES ACT, 2013 (‘THE 
ACT’)
The following Explanatory Statement sets out all 
material facts relating to the business mentioned 
under Item No. 4 in the accompanying Notice 
dated May 20, 2026.
Item No. 4
In terms of amended Regulation 24A of the Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and 
Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“ SEBI 
Listing Regulations ”), the Board of Directors of the 
Company has recommended the appointment of M/s 
DPV & Associates LLP, Company Secretaries (Firm 
Registration No. L2021HR009500), as the Secretarial 
Auditor of the Company for a term of five consecutive 
financial years commencing from April 1, 2026 up 
to March 31, 2031, subject to the approval of the 
Members at the ensuing Annual General Meeting.
Since the Company got listed on November 10, 2025 
and pursuant to amendment in Regulation 24A of 
the SEBI Listing Regulations, every listed company 
is now required to appoint either an individual for 
not more than one term of five consecutive years or 
a secretarial audit firm for not more than two terms 
of five consecutive years as the Secretarial Auditor 
based on the recommendation of its Board and 
subject to the approval of its Members in Annual 
General Meeting. Further, in terms of the aforesaid 
provisions, the appointment of Secretarial Auditors 
for a term of five consecutive years requires approval 
of the Members. A Secretarial Auditor is required to 
be a peer-reviewed Company Secretary and must 
not have incurred any disqualification as prescribed 
under applicable SEBI regulations.
After evaluating and considering various factors 
such as the firm’s experience, expertise, professional 
standing, peer review status, industry knowledge and 
capability to conduct secretarial audits of listed entities, 
the Board of Directors at its meeting held on May 20, 
2026 approved and recommended the appointment 
of M/s DPV & Associates LLP, Practising Company 
Secretaries (Firm Registration No. L2021HR009500), 
as the Secretarial Auditor of the Company for a term 
of five consecutive financial years commencing from 
April 1, 2026 and ending on March 31, 2031, subject 
to the approval of the Members.Brief Profile
M/s DPV & Associates LLP was founded by CS Devesh 
Vasisht (FCS No. 8488, CP No. 13700), a Fellow 
Member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of 
India, with over 18 years of experience in secretarial 
audit and a broad spectrum of corporate secretarial 
matters. The firm is a well established professional 
services provider, comprising a team of qualified 
Company Secretaries and experienced professionals 
of more than 12 members including 3 partners and 
it has strong expertise in secretarial audits, corporate 
governance, IPO advisory, due diligence, legal drafting, 
issuance of legal opinions, corporate restructuring, 
related party transactions, compounding of offences, 
and advising clients on compliance with the SEBI 
Regulations and other applicable corporate laws.
The firm has significant experience in conducting 
secretarial audits and advising large listed 
companies, including entities forming part of 
leading market-capitalisation based indices and 
governance frameworks prescribed under the SEBI 
Listing Regulations.
The firm is peer-reviewed and meets the eligibility 
criteria prescribed under Regulation 24A(1A) of the 
SEBI Listing Regulations.
M/s DPV & Associates LLP has provided its consent 
for the appointment and confirmed that it meets 
the applicable eligibility requirements and satisfies 
the independence criteria prescribed under the 
applicable laws, regulations and guidelines issued by 
the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.
The recommendation for the appointment of M/s 
DPV & Associates LLP as Secretarial Auditor is based 
on their past track record and capabilities in delivering 
quality secretarial audit services to Lenskart Solutions 
Limited and other companies of similar size and 
complexity. The proposed fee for Secretarial Audit 
is ` 2,50,000 (Rupees Two Lakh Fifty Thousand only) 
per annum plus applicable taxes and reimbursement 
of out-of-pocket expenses actually incurred in 
connection with the Audit of the Company with 
power to the Board to revise during the term.
None of the Directors, Key Managerial Personnel or 
their respective relatives are concerned or interested 
in the Resolution mentioned at Item No. 4 of the Notice.
The Board recommends the Resolution as set out 
at Item No. 4 of the accompanying Notice for the 
approval by the Members of the Company by way of 
an Ordinary Resolution.

Same Mission. 
Bigger Ambition.CEO’s Message
Dear Shareholders,
In FY26, Lenskart became a public company and 
crossed 50 million people served. But I do not think of either as a finish line. Around the world, 4 billion people need better vision, and most still do not get tested often enough, do not find eyewear inspiring, or do not receive the quality, price, and service they deserve. Our mission remains the same: to make quality eyewear accessible to all. Our long-term vision is to impact a billion people.
Let me share how we think about what Lenskart  
is becoming.Eyewear is fundamental to how people live and how 
they express themselves. It is essential for seeing the world clearly, and it is one of the first things others notice about you. We want people to see eyewear differently: not as something they buy once and forget, but as something they enjoy, something they choose for every occasion, every mood, every stage of life. Fashionable eyewear that improves quality of life through choice, styles, and self-expression. That is why we are building a house of brands - John Jacobs, Owndays, Meller, Hooper, and more to come - each serving a distinct customer and occasion, all powered by the Lenskart platform.
To deliver this, we are building a full-stack system 
that owns the customer journey end-to-end: from discovery to eye test, from design to manufacturing, from the in-store experience to delivery and lifelong care. AI works as an operating layer, turning every interaction into intelligence that makes the next one better. Technology amplifies the human experience, so that a person in a small town receives the same quality of care as someone in a metro. And over time, as eyewear evolves into a health and intelligence platform, we are building the foundation to lead that transition too.
That is our long-term vision: Vision for a Billion. 
Our immediate goal is 100 million - the rest follows from there. FY26 gave us real proof that we are on the right path.
The business is compounding. Revenue, margins, 
and reinvestment capacity all improved together. We opened 603 net new stores, funded largely from operating cash flows. We launched B by Lenskart, our first AI-powered smart glasses, opening a new category where eyewear becomes intelligent.
The opportunity in India is enormous. Hundreds of 
millions of people still lack access to quality eye care. In FY26, we saw our model work deeper into the country than ever before. Stores in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns are thriving. Remote optometry is unlocking access in places where it was previously unavailable. We believe we have barely scratched the surface.
We are also building Lenskart into a global consumer 
brand. We believe, that for a consumer brand to stay relevant and continuously raise its standards, it must become global. Being present across markets keeps us at the forefront of innovation, exposes us to fast-changing consumer preferences, and constantly elevates our quality. In FY26, Japan delivered record growth. We now serve customers over 16 countries. Each market teaches us something new, and that learning flows back into everything we do.
Underneath all of this are the systems. 
Our manufacturing delivers innovative eyewear at competitive prices, high quality, and increasing speed. Our 3,300+ stores operate as testing centres, service hubs, and last-mile nodes. Our data systems, built on over 24 million eye tests and years of customer interactions, compound every day. And our 20,000+ people across 30+ nationalities make these systems better every single day.
We remain early. The public markets bring greater 
responsibility, but they do not change our orientation. We will work hard every day to build something that matters, something that lasts, and something that changes how a billion people experience vision.
It is still Day Zero.Peyush Bansal

Redefining Eyewear 
Through an Integrated, Intelligent PlatformIntroducing Lenskart
Lenskart is a technology-driven eyewear company built around a simple but powerful need: helping people see better and experience the world with greater clarity. Our aim is to provide ‘Eyewear for All’ and make quality eyeglasses more accessible and affordable across our operating markets.
Redefining eyewear through an integrated, intelligent platformIndia’s Most Trusted Eyewear Brand of 2025
1
1Recognised by TRA Research
Annual Report 2025-26

=== page 29 ===
We bring together design, manufacturing, 
technology, supply chain and retail to create an integrated eyewear platform designed to serve the everyday vision needs of customers across age groups, price points, occasions and geographies. Our model is direct-to-consumer, omnichannel and data-led, enabling customers to discover, try, buy, receive and service eyewear across digital and physical touchpoints.
Lenskart’s vertically integrated model has been 
built around that journey. Digital discovery creates intent. Eye tests make the need visible. Stores, home try-on and app journeys reduce friction. Design and brand capabilities make eyewear more expressive. Manufacturing, centralised inventory and fulfilment protect quality, speed and affordability. Service systems keep trust alive after purchase.
Beyond making vision accessible, we want to 
improve the quality of life of the people who wear our eyewear. That means pushing the bar on what eyewear itself can be – creating unique eyewear built for the specific moments in people’s lives, from weddings to work to holidays. Eyewear has long been the most unevolved lifestyle category: unlike shoes, apparel, and accessories, which have continually reinvented themselves through design and innovation, eyewear largely has not. We intend to transform the way people experience the world through eyewear – and we do that by continuing to raise the bar with new products  
and eyewear brands.Technology and AI are the bridge across these elements. They help us understand where demand exists, what customers may like, how stores should operate, where eye tests can be conducted, how products should be routed, and how customer issues should be resolved. As our platform scales, we are evolving from a technology-driven eyewear company to a data-driven consumer technology company, in which every interaction strengthens the system. 
This integrated system also provides the 
foundation for building a global consumer brand. We believe for a consumer brand to remain relevant and continually raise its standards, it must go global. In lifestyle categories, global brands leverage cross-market learning to anticipate consumer shifts, adapt faster, and become the preferred choice over time. Being global keeps us at the forefront - Singapore drives our myopia control expertise, Thailand sharpens our fashion sensibility, and Japan elevates our quality standards. We are not an ‘NRI-only brand’, our proposition resonates with local consumers. Our goal is to become the #1 brand in each market. 
The same capabilities that help us serve 
customers in India are being adapted across international markets, supported by local insights, global brand thinking, and a consistent focus on the customer experience. The result is not a separate technology story. It is a more intelligent eyewear platform built to make vision care simpler, more personal and more accessible.

A Growing Global Problem,  
Still UnderservedMarket Overview
Prevalence 
Vision correction is one of the world’s largest unmet consumer needs. As of 31st March 2025, 
approximately 4 billion individuals globally required vision correction for refractive errors. Of these, 
approximately 2 billion individuals did not use prescription eyewear. In India, approximately 0.8 billion needed vision correction in FY25, growing to approximately 0.9 billion in FY30.

=== page 31 ===
Many customers do not have easy access to 
optometrists or organised eyewear stores. Others delay the purchase because of cost, limited product choice, inconsistent quality, poor guidance or long delivery timelines.
For us, this isn’t just a market, it’s a fundamental 
human need. And we believe we are not just participating in this market, we are catalysing market creation. In FY26, we conducted 23.8 million eye tests across our markets, up 48.5% YoY. But here’s the number that matters most to us. In India, approximately half of these were first-time eye exams. People who didn’t know they needed vision correction until we made eye testing accessible. The majority of them discovered a prescription issue and bought their first pair of glasses at Lenskart.Reaching the customers through Stores 
While the problem of refractive errors is growing and there is strong latent demand, optical store density remains very low, creating a hindrance for consumers looking to get eye tests. There is significant potential for store addition to address this latent demand driven by low market penetration and the rising incidence of refractive errors. One of the key challenges behind this low density has been the limited penetration of organised players, led by complexities in both the manufacturing supply chain and eye testing – each requiring highly skilled manpower.

=== page 33 ===
2. Remote Eye Testing
We have deployed remote eye testing in 623 stores in India and even Japan now, allowing one 
optometrist to serve multiple locations using AI-enabled co-pilots with a high degree of efficiency and quality. Our vision correction professionals connect with customers in-store and control the diagnostic equipment from a distance to conduct precise eye tests. Our Centre of Excellence in Kolkata acts as a hub for this model, enabling optometrists to conduct eye tests for customers across locations. By using centralised expertise more effectively, we are improving optometrist productivity, reducing dependence on local optometrist availability and making high-quality eye testing more scalable across smaller towns and underserved catchments.
We also extended access to eye tests for children aged 8+ across our stores in India, supported 
by proprietary technology that validates multiple prescriptions with child-specific modifications. This helps us identify vision correction needs earlier and make eye care more accessible across age groups.1.  Geo IQ
 Our AI platform GeoIQ analyses 3,000+ plus variables to identify optical locations, ensuring disciplined expansion and low paybacks. 
3. Centralised Supply Chain
We have built a centralised technology-led supply chain that delivers next day in 78 cities and now even same day in some cities. Behind every pair of glasses we ship, there’s a network of automation and AI solving real problems at scale.

=== page 34 ===
Sizing the Opportunity: India’s Expanding Eyewear Market 
Starting from population and working through to market value, arrives us at 242 million pairs and 
`788 billion size of Indian eyewear market in FY25. FY26 is estimated to be `894 billion.
According to data published by the Directorate 
General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (Ministry of Commerce and Industry, GOI), India imported 440 million ophthalmic lenses in FY25 (~220 million pairs). This aligns directionally with Redseer’s estimate of 242 million pairs of prescription eyeglasses sold in India during the same period. Further, the same government data shows that 237 million units (~118 million pairs) were imported in FY19, indicating a volume CAGR of 11% between FY19 and FY25 further validating the robust growth of prescription eyeglasses industry in India.We believe the current market size of `894 
billion understates the opportunity because it only measures existing behaviour and not the latent demand. When organised players began the process of establishing stores and offering professional eye tests, they were able to reach a large segment of the population who were previously unaware of their need for vision correction. Consequently, industry market estimates have expanded significantly over the last decade (from `35 billion to `550–850 
billion). We believe this considerable expansion is not only due to increase in vision issues, but the result of organised optical retail’s effort to validate and uncover the true size of the underlying, latent consumer demand.
Lenskart is not merely participating in the 
market; we are catalysing market creation. With over 770 million Indians needing vision correction, we recognise that the market’s true potential is elastic: it grows exponentially as our accessible model converts this massive, latent need into active consumer demand.Building Block FY25E FY30E

=== page 42 ===
Technology-Led, 
AI-Enabled Intelligence across the Value Chain Foundations of Our Vertically Integrated Platform 
Eyewear is a deeply personal category. Every customer has a different face, prescription, style preference, purchase behaviour and service need. Solving this at scale requires more than reach. It requires a system that can understand these differences, learn continuously and make every interaction better than the last.
At Lenskart, we do not see 
technology as a separate layer of the 
business. We see it as the operating 
system that drives how we build eyewear. It shapes how we design products, guide discovery, conduct eye tests, personalise recommendations, manufacture made-to-prescription eyewear, fulfil orders and serve customers across markets.
Technology and AI are the connective layer across this journey. It helps us to move from standardised journeys to more responsive ones; from a broad assortment to personalised choice; from reactive service to faster resolution; and from experience-led decisions to data-backed execution.
Our stores are also part of this integrated system. They are not inventory showcases. They act as 
neighbourhood access points and order-booking engines, supported by centralised manufacturing, supply chain and digital infrastructure. This allows us to offer the reach of physical retail while operating with a more asset-light, scalable model.
As we scale globally, this intelligence becomes even more important. It helps us stay close to local 
customer needs while operating with the consistency, speed, and quality of a single integrated platform. It also supports operating leverage, as earlier investments in technology, manufacturing and data systems serve a larger base of customers and transactions.
The pages that follow show how this philosophy comes to life across the six pillars of our 
integrated platform:

Rewiring the 
Eyewear Value ChainCentralised Supply Chain
Bhiwadi: Scaling Precision Manufacturing
Our Bhiwadi facility is a key part of our centralised manufacturing 
and supply chain model. It supports prescription eyewear production across procurement, lens coating, edging, cutting, polishing, assembly and dispatch.
The facility is among the top two vertically integrated centralised 
manufacturing facilities for prescription eyeglasses globally, in terms of FY25 manufacturing capacity. With 75% automation, including fully automated robotic surfacing and automated dispatch and delivery systems, Bhiwadi helps us maintain quality control, prescription accuracy and faster service for customers.
FY2410.117.5
13.2
FY25 FY26Prescription eyeglasses 
manufactured at just-in-time centralised facilities (Mn) vs distributedTraditionally, eyewear is manufactured and assembled across 
stores or local labs, with lenses processed and fitted closer to the point of sale. This approach not only relies heavily on manual intervention, but makes it difficult to achieve consistent quality, precision and speed.
We have reimagined this model through a centralised, 
technology-enabled manufacturing ecosystem. Powered by our in-house developed warehouse management system, NexS, every order is digitally orchestrated through a single integrated facility, enabling consistent quality, greater precision and faster fulfillment.

Our Home Try-on (HTO)
For an elderly customer who cannot walk to the 
store to get their eyes tested, or anyone unwilling to step out into the summer heat just to try on a pair of glasses, buying eyewear has always meant trading convenience for confidence. Home Try-on removes that trade-off, the store comes home instead.
A trained Lenskart vision care professional 
visits the customer at home, brings a curated set of frames, performs a 12-step eye check, and helps the customer choose and order – all without leaving home. No queuing. No rushing. Full personal attention in a familiar setting, with frames tried in natural light and a mirror the customer already trusts.
In FY26, HTO operated across 1,000+ pincodes. 
The service converted attended customers at very high rates, meaningfully above walk-in or purely digital rates. HTO’s NPS came in a couple of points higher than the overall Lenskart India.

sites, and shortlist opportunities through a single intelligence stack. Its “find the best market for me” engine will help shift expansion planning from reactive site evaluation to proactive market targeting.

ManufacturingIn the traditional eyewear model, a pair of glasses passes through multiple hands before reaching the 
customer: manufacturer, importer, wholesaler, distributor and retailer. Each layer can add time, cost and complexity.
We have taken a more direct path.Lenskart began by building a direct-to-consumer supply chain, connecting suppliers and customers 
through one platform. We are now moving further upstream, manufacturing more frames and lenses in-house and selling directly through our omnichannel network.
Stores stay focussed on the customer-facing moments: discovery, eye tests, assistance and order 
booking. Behind them, our centralised supply chain carries out the precision work, from procurement, coating, edging, cutting, and polishing to assembly, sortation, and fulfilment.
This model works only when centralisation is matched with speed. The customer promise depends 
on designing the right products, manufacturing prescription eyewear accurately, placing inventory intelligently, sorting orders quickly and delivering reliably. The Next Form 
Factor: Eyewear as Wearable Intelligence
46Annual Report 2025-26

=== page 63 ===
The form factor of eyewear is undergoing a profound evolution, shifting from traditional 
vision-correction tools into “wearable intelligence” designed for everyday life. Because eyewear sits on a person’s face for twelve or more hours a day, it maintains a persistent physical proximity to the human body that no other consumer device can replicate. This unique positioning makes it the ideal next-generation medium to seamlessly integrate technology into daily life.
Through B by Lenskart, our AI-powered, prescription-capable smart glasses integrated with Google 
Gemini Live, we are actively pursuing this shift. Initial customer rollouts have validated this new design canvas, with users highly praising the product’s ultra-lightweight fit and comfort, premium low-light photo and video capture, and upgraded audio quality. Early feedback also highlighted a premium unboxing experience and the immense convenience of an on-the-go charging cable that keeps the device powered without relying on a bulky case.
As we iterate on future form factors that will include advanced display capabilities, a critical pillar 
remains unchanged: smart glasses must still fulfil their core medical function of prescription vision correction. By leveraging our deep prescription expertise and vast network of physical stores, Lenskart ensures consumers can experience, purchase, and service these tech-enabled frames seamlessly.

=== page 69 ===
Lenskart Academy trains, certifies, 
and continuously coaches every Lenskartian who goes on the floor to talk to customer. Whether they are store associates, store managers or optometrists – everyone gets trained.Lenskart Academy: Empowering 
Customer-First Excellence
1,200+
Monthly learner capacity
Up from 650 last year
488
Training programmes delivered FY26
The most expensive mistake in retail training 
is sending someone to the shop floor before they're ready. Earlier, there used to be no alternative – a new hire's first real practice used to be a real customer, live, with real consequences if something went wrong.
That has now changed. During classroom 
training, every learner completes AI-powered roleplays at the end of each day. These simulations recreate demanding customer situations, including cart abandonment, delivery complaints, multiple simultaneous conversations, unfamiliar technical queries, styling consultations and warranty concerns. The AI doesn't play just one customer – it plays many: a rushed businessman, an undecided elderly shopper, a first-time buyer who needs everything explained twice, so learners get comfortable with the actual range of people who walk into a store, not one idealised persona. The system tracks exactly where they hesitate, oversell, or fall short on product knowledge. For the customer, that always means the experience feels like it's coming from someone experienced, even on their first day.
Similarly, an optometrist runs more than 100 
practice eye tests before their first real one. The customer gets someone who's already done this before.AI-Rehearsals Before

=== page 77 ===
India BusinessBusiness Performance and Outlook
India is where the Lenskart model is most deeply established and most visible at scale. In FY26, 
India revenue grew 33.7% YoY to `52,648 million, driven by sustained volume expansion and new customer acquisition.
India’s FY26 growth was led by four mutually reinforcing factors. First, sustained volume expansion 
was supported by eye tests that converted latent need into active demand. Second, a deepening customer franchise, with Gold membership, digital influence and new collections strengthening repeat engagement. Third, a modest ASP step-up, driven by premiumisation across frames, lenses and sunglasses. Fourth, continued improvement in customer experience through faster delivery, better store journeys and stronger service.
This is the core of our India model: we are not only competing for existing demand; we are expanding 
the market by making eye testing, product choice, affordability and fulfillment more accessible.
Same Store Growth
India delivered 20.8% Same Store Sales Growth and 27.3% Same-Pincode Sales Growth in FY26. The gap between SSSG and SPSG is an important signal: new stores are expanding demand within micro-markets, rather than simply shifting customers from existing stores.
This gives us greater confidence in our densification model. As our store network deepens, 
each new store improves proximity, convenience and customer trust, while the overall pincode continues to grow.
Store Expansion
In FY26, we added 542 net new stores in India, nearly double the 282 added in FY25. We entered 157 new cities, expanded our presence to 556 cities and continued to deliver strong store performance. This expansion was guided by two signals: demand remains underpenetrated even in established markets, and the Tier 2+ opportunity is deeper than earlier estimated. GeoIQ-led site selection, cannibalisation modelling, remote optometry and our centralised supply chain helped us expand with discipline.
India’s eyewear opportunity is increasingly visible beyond the largest cities. Tier 2+ markets accounted 
for 254 of the 542 net new India stores in FY26, compared with 89 stores in FY25.
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements

=== page 78 ===
Profitability
India’s growth translated into stronger operating 
leverage. In FY26, India EBITDA grew 70.0% YoY to `10,675 million, with EBITDA margin at 20.3%. 
EBITDA (Pre-IndAS 116) grew 95.8% YoY to `7,535 million, with a margin of 14.3%.
This improvement reflects the structural 
benefits of our India model. Product margin remained strong, supported by scale, centralised manufacturing and backward integration. Marketing cost reduced as a percentage of revenue, reflecting stronger brand pull, Gold-led repeat behaviour, digital influence and sharper customer acquisition. Other expenses also declined as a percentage of revenue, supported by technology-led operating leverage and lower relative franchise/FOFO commission intensity as the store mix evolved.
Technology also helped reduce the cost-to-
serve. GeoIQ improved expansion discipline. Face recognition, AI-led recommendations, automated service workflows, and store operating systems improved both productivity and the experience. As revenue scales, these systems allow central costs to spread over a larger base, supporting margin expansion without compromising growth.India remains significantly underpenetrated 
for organised eyewear. We serve around 25 million eyewear units annually, while India needs more than 700 million, leaving a long runway for market creation.
In FY27, we expect net new store additions 
to remain at or around FY26 levels. Our focus will remain on sustaining growth through higher eye-test penetration, first-time customer acquisition, remote and self-optometry, Tier 2+ expansion, digitally influenced demand, Gold-led repeat behaviour, premium lenses, advanced coatings, myopia management, faster fulfilment and newer categories such as smart eyewear.
We will continue to track annual volume 
growth as the clearest indicator of underlying market expansion, while using technology, AI and operating discipline to expand access with stronger efficiency.

Southeast Asia: Dual-Brand Strategy 
Driving Consolidation
Southeast Asia is not one market. It is a set of 
distinct consumer opportunities shaped by different retail structures, fashion preferences and adoption curves.
Singapore was our first international market and 
remains an important proof point. One in four Singaporeans wear our glasses. We operate a dual-brand strategy, with Owndays serving the premium segment and Lenskart expanding accessibility through a wider portfolio and Gold membership model. The proposition is deepening through contact lenses, self-order kiosks, faster delivery and high-street expansion.
Thailand brings a different opportunity. It is a 
fashion-forward market where Owndays has built strong traction, while Lenskart is being introduced with sharper design relevance. Collections such as Pop Mart have seen strong customer response, supported by local partnerships and fashion-led marketing.
Across Southeast Asia, we are executing 
a market-by-market consolidation and localisation strategy, with a growing presence across Malaysia, Cambodia, the Philippines, Vietnam and Indonesia.
Japan: Capturing the D2C Shift in a 
Mature Market
Japan is our largest international market and an 
important learning ground for quality, service and store discipline.
Through Owndays, we are participating in 
a market where consumers are increasingly moving towards value-focussed D2C brands. The opportunity is not only to expand stores, but to deepen same store performance, integrate supply chains and use technology to strengthen the customer journey.
AI-led store analytics and remote optometry 
are already supporting the operating model. GeoIQ analysis also highlights whitespace in underpenetrated prefectures, giving us a clearer view of where we can build regional density over time.
Japan raises our internal benchmarks, helping 
us improve product quality, store execution and customer experience across the wider Lenskart platform.

The World we SeeFocus on Sustainability
Clear sight can change the course of a life, whether it belongs to a child trying to learn, a worker trying 
to earn, or an elderly person trying to stay independent. Vision is not merely a sense. It is access.
A blurry world should not be anyone’s reality.
Yet today, one in two people lack clear vision, and half of them still do not have access to something as simple as a pair of glasses.
1
The Lancet Global Health estimates that the annual global productivity loss due to vision impairment and blindness is $410.7
2 billion. Beyond costs, the impact of this crisis is even more profound, visible 
in learning, livelihoods and everyday independence.
Research shows that up to 80% of what a child learns in their early school years is presented visually3. 
When children with uncorrected vision receive a simple pair of glasses, their reading scores improve 
significantly, often matching the impact of months of additional schooling.4
1  “Industry Report on the Eyewear Market” dated October 15, 2025, prepared by Redseer Strategy Consultants Private Limited for 
L
enskart Prospectus, available at https://static.lenskart.com/media/desktop/corporate/IPO-IndustryReport.pdf
2  The Lancet Global Health, “Global economic productivity losses from vision impairment and blindness,” 2021.  
A
vailable at: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8093883/
3  UCLA / Vision to Learn study (Slusser & Dudovitz, 2013, Mattel Children’s Hospital, UCLA), available at  
h
ttps://visiontolearn.org/impact/ucla-study-impact-analysis-of-vision-to-learn/
4  Johns Hopkins University, “Eyeglasses for school students help improve academic achievement,” 2021. Available at:  
h
ttps://schoolhealth.jhu.edu/2021/09/1700/
At Lenskart, we believe that clear vision is 
a fundamental human right, not a privilege. We exist to close this gap and transform the way people see and experience the world. This is our “Vision for a Billion.”

Sustainability Issues that

Vision as a Right, Not a Privilege
One of the single largest barriers to vision care 
globally is access. Every eye test at a Lenskart store globally is completely free, removing cost as the first barrier to someone even finding out they need vision correction.
Further, technology is how we close that gap at 
scale: in FY26, in India we equipped 623 stores with remote eye-testing, a 271% increase in a single year. Through remote optometry, a single qualified optometrist can now serve customers hundreds of kilometres away, extending expert diagnosis into towns that have never had one. It also creates flexible, location-independent livelihoods for optometry talent.
We complement this with physical reach, 
growing our network across the globe from 1,959 stores in FY23 to 3,327 stores in FY26. In India, our presence in Tier 2+ and smaller towns nearly doubled from 483 to 952 stores, while Tier 1 cities more than doubled from 277 to 614 stores.And beyond our commercial network, the Lenskart Foundation extends this reach further still, into underserved rural communities through initiatives like Drishti – Har Gaon, Har Ghar and mobile eye-care units, bringing screening and correction to each and everyone.
Reaching Those Who Cannot Reach Us
For the elderly, the differently abled, and those 
without easy transport, we bring the optometrist to the doorstep through our at-home eye-test service, supported by next-day delivery across 78 Indian cities.
Consistent quality – Metro to Remote
Every pair of glasses delivered in India is 
manufactured at Lenskart’s vertically integrated facilities in Bhiwadi or Manesar, Gurugram. This integrated manufacturing model enables us to deliver the same high standards of quality and precision to every customer, irrespective of where they are located across the country.

Community Impact: India
Our community in India work runs through the 
Lenskart Foundation, built on the conviction that vision is a right, not a privilege. Giving back to the community is a fundamental aspect of our corporate ethos. As a responsible corporate citizen, we are dedicated to undertaking initiatives beyond our business operations, focussed on the overall benefit and development of local communities and society.
We have established a comprehensive 
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) policy to guide and ensure the effective implementation of our community outreach efforts. Our CSR interventions primarily focus on providing preventive eye healthcare to underprivileged and economically disadvantaged segments of society.
We fulfil our CSR responsibilities through the 
Lenskart Foundation, a not-for-profit charitable organisation committed to raising awareness and eradicating refractive-error-induced blindness nationwide, leveraging technology as a key enabler.
Project: Drishti Didi 
Our flagship project, the 
Drishti Didis initiative, seeks to revolutionise eye care in rural areas by establishing 'Women Eye Marshals' in every village across the nation. These local women, known as 'Drishti Didis,' receive training from Lenskart to conduct preliminary eye tests and relay vision data to our team. Based on this data, our specialists then perform comprehensive eye exams and provide necessary spectacles.

The Lenskart Foundation continues to advance our purpose of making vision accessible to all, 
focussed on expanding primary eye care in underserved and rural communities. The Drishti – Har Gaon, Har Ghar programme, a women-led model for last-mile eye screening and vision correction – has onboarded over 1,000 Drishti Didis across 940 villages in five states, screened more than 910,000 individuals, provided eyeglasses to over 42,000+ people, and made 351 villages refractive-error free.
Our goal is to train 50,000 Drishti Didis, extending 'Drishti Har Gaon Har Ghar' to every village in 
the five states where we currently operate, and to broaden the initiative to new states over time. To support this, we are establishing four Eye Care Centres in each of the five active states.
This is inclusion compounding on itself: vision care reaching the unreached, delivered by women who earn a livelihood from it. Each Drishti Didi receives a structured honorarium tied to screenings conducted, turning community health work into a dependable, flexible income source close to home.A Livelihood Story, not Just

In July 2023, we introduced our

Okinawa School Vision Support Programme
In Japan, school health checks routinely identify 
children with uncorrected vision. The challenge is often not diagnosis, but affordability. As children move through primary school, the cost of replacing glasses year after year can become a barrier for families.
Through the Elementary School Academic 
Support Project, OWNDAYS provides free prescription eyewear to children who fail school vision screenings across Okinawa and Kumamoto. Since 2022, eligible children have been entitled to one new pair of glasses each year as they advance a grade, for up to six pairs through primary school.The programme has scaled steadily, from 503 children in 2022 to 3,489 children in 2025, crossing 7,853 children supported cumulatively. Announced in March 2026, Naha City, Ginowan City and Kitanakagusuku Village joined the programme, extending its reach to 18 municipalities and covering an estimated 77.7% of Okinawa Prefecture’s population.
The glasses are designed for daily school use – 
lightweight, allergy-tested TR-90 resin frames and thin aspheric lenses.
The aim is simple: fewer children held back by 
uncorrected vision and fewer families forced to choose between a child’s eyesight and other living costs.

Inclusivity by Design
For decades, the eyewear industry has largely 
been shaped by standardised assumptions around fit, affordability and style, often overlooking the diverse needs and preferences of individual customers. As a result, millions have had limited access to eyewear solutions that genuinely reflect their unique facial features, lifestyles and personal expression.
Designing for Identity
Our Turban Fit range is a clear example. 
Standard frames can dig into a turban or sit uncomfortably against it. Turban Fit uses ultra-thin temples designed to slide into the turban without pressure or disruption, addressing a small daily friction for a community that eyewear design has often overlooked.A House of Brands for Distinct Lives
One brand cannot serve every taste, need and 
budget. Our portfolio allows us to reach different customer groups with greater relevance, from John Jacobs in affordable-premium eyewear and Aqualens in contact lenses to international brands such as Owndays and Meller, which extend our reach across geographies, categories and styles.
Celebrating Indian Art and Craft
Lenskart's design language often draws 
inspiration from India's rich visual heritage. The Gulmarg collection reinterprets Kashmiri craftsmanship through carved motifs and intricate lattice-inspired frame details, while Indian Accent celebrates bold metallic silhouettes, striking geometries, and rich royal hues with a distinctly Indian aesthetic. By translating regional design traditions into contemporary eyewear, these collections give Indian customers a homegrown brand they are proud to wear.
Peyush Bansal, our Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer, won “Entrepreneur of the Year” at the Forbes India Leadership Awards 2026. This added to earlier recognitions as “Entrepreneur of the Year” at The Economic Times Awards for Corporate Excellence and “Innovator of the Year” at NDTV Indian of the Year.

Sustainability, Lived from the Ground Up
Owning more of the eyewear value chain gives 
us a clearer view of our environmental footprint. From design, manufacturing and logistics to stores, packaging and waste, we can see where resources are used and where impact can be reduced.
This gives us the ability to act with discipline: 
improving energy efficiency, reducing waste, managing water responsibly and building circularity into everyday operations.Climate, energy, water, waste and circularity are not five separate initiatives for us. They are five areas where the same instinct applies: run tighter, plan better and waste less. The discipline that keeps our unit economics healthy is the same discipline that helps keep our footprint 
smaller than it would otherwise be.
We do not treat sustainability as a separate 
initiative. For us, as a vertically integrated company, the same habits that lower cost and reduce waste also help us grow more efficiently and responsibly.

Through initiatives promoting tree plantation, climate literacy and responsible consumption, we encouraged employees to strengthen their commitment to sustainable practices, reinforcing that lasting environmental impact begins with everyday choices. Our environmental strategy is anchored in a 
clear long-term commitment: net zero GHG Emission by 2050.

Transport & Logistics
Our logistics network and last-mile sortation are

engagement helps us work with partners on 
measuring and reducing their footprint, extending

Climate Risk & Resilience
Climate risks affect our business in different 
ways, depending on location, asset type and time horizon. We assess both the physical risks of a changing climate and the transition risks that arise as we move towards a lower-carbon economy, in line with the IFRS S2 framework.
Physical Risk, Mapped to the Location
We assess climate risk at a location-specific 
level, recognising that flood risk in Bhiwadi and cyclone exposure on the coast are not the same problem.
Our analysis considers coastal inundation,  
gradual flooding, pluvial flooding, cyclone 
intensity and heat under moderated and business-as-usual climate scenarios, up to  
Year 2100.

  Supply

logistics routes, supported by a centralised 
inventory model, so deliveries can keep moving even when one route is disrupted
●
  Ener
gy-efficient cooling: Continued 
focus on efficient cooling and renewable power use at our manufacturing facilities in Bhiwadi and Gurugram, where precision lens manufacturing depends on controlled conditions and worker productivity is directly exposed to rising heat

=== page 110 ===
In FY26, we generated 2,683 MT of waste, of 
which 73% was recycled.
For us, circularity starts with a simple idea: 
eyewear should become more accessible without becoming more wasteful. We focus on three points in the value chain: how we manage waste inside our factories, how we extend the life of our products and how we reduce the impact of packaging.
In Our Operations
At Bhiwadi, one of the things we do is to create 
infrastructure from the waste we generated, when we cut lens blanks, the process leaves behind monomer waste, which we repurpose into material for the plant’s own internal roads, instead of sending it to landfill, and avoiding the emissions that come from quarrying virgin material for the same road. Across our factories, almost all of our waste is non-hazardous, and almost all of it goes to recycling partners instead of a landfill.
In Our Products
We are designing circularity into how customers 
use and maintain eyewear.
●
 
 Our
 Free Lens Replacement initiative allows 
customers to replace lenses without replacing 
the frame, extending the life of each pair
● 
 For
 children, our modular, swappable- 
component frames allow specific parts to be replaced as faces and prescriptions change, reducing the need to discard the full frame
● 
  Our
 take-back programme allows customers 
to return old eyewear for recycling or donation, helping close the loop with the person who actually wore the product
Meller: Sustainable  
Materials and Packaging
Meller, our Barcelona-based digital-first 
sunglasses brand, shows how sustainability can be built into design choices, material selection and packaging without compromising product quality.
Most Meller frames use G850, a bio-based 
polymer with approximately 45% bio-based carbon content derived from castor oil, a renewable, non-food agricultural resource. This reduces dependence on fossil-based plastic while retaining the durability expected from everyday eyewear. Meller also offers a Bio-acetate premium line, crafted from organic materials as an alternative to traditional acetate.
The brand’s design approach also supports 
longevity. Every Meller model is unisex by design, helping reduce overproduction and extending the relevance of each frame across a wider base of customers. All sunglasses carry UV400 protection and polarised lenses as standard, making quality a built-in feature rather than an add-on.
Packaging follows the same principle. 
Meller uses FSC-certified paper boxes, W, and pouches and cleaning cloths made from 100% recycled PET (RPET). The use of FSC-certified paper supports responsible forest management, biodiversity protection and sustainable sourcing, while recycled plastics help extend the life of post-consumer materials and reduce dependence on virgin plastic.
These choices make sustainability part of how 
the product is designed, sourced and shipped, with improvements made year after year.

Governance
Scale without discipline can create complexity. 
As we grow across manufacturing, retail, logistics and digital channels, governance helps ensure that decisions are made with accountability, clarity and long-term responsibility.
For us, governance is not a compliance exercise. 
It is how we build trust, protect the interests of stakeholders and keep the business resilient as it scales. Our ESG approach is integrated into this governance structure, with oversight across risk, performance, disclosures and responsible business practices.
Suppliers and Business Partners
Our relationships with suppliers are built on a structured, transparent procurement framework. Every new vendor goes through formal due diligence and an on-site factory visit before a single order is placed. This includes verification of regulatory and statutory compliance, review of past legal or regulatory issues and submission of Conflict-of-Interest declarations.
Supplier selection follows competitive, 
multi-vendor processes, including e-bidding, to support fairness and transparency. Expectations are documented through agreements and service-level terms before engagement begins.
Supplier accountability continues beyond 
onboarding. Every supplier goes through an annual Vendor Performance Evaluation on  
quality, delivery, and professionalism. Future business allocation is linked to this score, making supplier accountability continuous, measurable and tied to performance.
Supplier ESG Assessment
We took this further in FY26 by conducting a 
structured ESG assessment across our select suppliers. The assessment used a comprehensive questionnaire, scored out of 100, with a methodology aligned to established frameworks such as EcoVadis and DJSI. Each supplier was classified from “Beginner” to “Exemplary” based on their performance.The objective was not only to rank suppliers, but to support measurable improvement. Each supplier received a scorecard and a specific, actionable improvement plan, with next steps such as computing their own Scope 3 emissions or working towards ISO 50001 and ISO 14001 certification. We also conducted an ESG capability-building workshop for our procurement team, ensuring that supplier engagement is backed by a clear internal understanding of what strong ESG performance looks like.
We also tightened the process side of supplier 
management this year. Vendor onboarding moved further onto AI-enabled workflows built into our ERP, cutting down manual review and making domestic and international onboarding more consistent with each other. This is part of the wider direction we are taking across procurement: tighter systems, cleaner data and less room for inconsistency in how suppliers are assessed, onboarded and managed.
Data Security & Customer Privacy
Lenskart was built digitally before it was built in physical retail. We launched our website in 2010, before opening our first store in Delhi in 2013. That legacy of “think online” still shapes how we manage customer data.
Our website and app are not just sales channels. 
They carry transactions, prescriptions, service requests and customer interactions at scale. As we have grown into a technology-enabled omnichannel business, this foundation has extended into newer use cases, including AI-led recommendations, face-geometry scans and in-store analytics.
Privacy and security are therefore embedded 
into our daily operations. We manage data protection through formal policies, privacy-by-design principles, strengthened cybersecurity systems and oversight by a dedicated Data Protection Officer aligned with India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act.
Annual Report 2025-26
96
=== page 113 ===
Anonymisation In Our In-Store Analytics
Our AI-led computer vision platform 
analyses store traffic and performance while protecting privacy at source. The system converts video footage into numerical data and deletes original images, so insights are derived from anonymised, aggregated information rather than identifiable visuals.
Consent and customer rights
Customers can access, correct, or delete their data and withdraw consent at any time through our dedicated 
Data Protection Officer, with special safeguards for the data of children and persons with disability.Safeguarding Facial Data In Our 3D Try-On
For 3D Try-On, customers are informed before 
facial scans are captured. This data is never shared with third parties and is used only to measure optical parameters, recommend better-fitting frames and improve services. In FY26, this translated into zero data breaches, 
zero cybersecurity complaints, and zero privacy-related non-compliance penalties.
Our Policies
Good intentions don’t survive scale unless they’re written down and enforced consistently. Our policy 
framework exists precisely for that reason. It helps ensure that transparency, ethical conduct and 
disciplined practice do not depend on individual judgement alone, but are embedded into the way we work across the organisation.Our Board of Directors

Our risk management framework is designed to support effective corporate governance, internal control and timely risk reporting. As the business evolves, the framework enables us to identify, assess, mitigate, monitor and report risks across its operations and value chain, drawing on internal assessments, operating experience, regulatory developments and changes in the external business environment.
Risks are assessed based on severity, control 
environment and likelihood of occurrence, enabling management attention and mitigation efforts to be prioritised. Risk responses may include accepting, avoiding, transferring or controlling the risk, supported by internal controls, process improvements, technology interventions, supplier diversification and contingency planning.
The Board oversees the risk management 
framework and periodically reviews the Company’s risk appetite and tolerance. The Risk Management Committee supports this oversight by monitoring existing and emerging risks, reviewing key risk metrics and performance against approved thresholds, and overseeing the implementation of risk-related policies. At Lenskart, we follow a three-lines-of-defence model: business and support functions own and manage risks day to day; the Risk Management Department provides guidance, oversight and consolidation; and internal audit provides independent assurance on the adequacy and effectiveness of risk management processes.

1281. Brief outline on CSR Policy of the Company:
  Lenskart Solutions Limited (the “Company”) is committed to the philosophy that vision is a fundamental 
human righ
t, and its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) policy is strategically designed to bridge the 
gap in accessible eye care across India. In alignment with Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Company’s initiatives are centered on the mission of providing “Vision for All” by leveraging its expertise in optical technology and supply chain management. This framework focuses on creating a sustainable social impact through preventive healthcare, specifically targeting the eradication of avoidable blindness and vision impairment among marginalized communities, while ensuring that all projects strictly adhere to the activities specified in Schedule VII of the Act.
  These s
trategic initiatives are primarily executed through the Lenskart Foundation (CSR Registration 
No: CSR00042891), which facilitates high-impact programs including Child Eye Care Centres for free diagnostics and the “Drishti Didi” initiative for training local women as primary eye-care workers. Furthermore, the Company deploys Mobile Vision Vans to reach remote rural locations, ensuring that quality eye care is delivered directly to those in need.

138Management Discussion and Analysis
1. The Market Context
1A. India
The Indian eyewear market is a nascent, fast-growing 
category in the early stages of its own creation. Over 700 million Indians require vision correction today, yet the current market size is estimated at approximately `894 billion. The addressable 
market is growing at 13% and is projected to exceed `4,000 billion by FY45. This gap is driven 
by two forces: the historically low penetration of eyeglasses, where a significant share of people who need corrective eyewear do not own a pair and the growing prevalence of refractive errors, accelerated by increased screen time and lifestyle evolution. When we talk about market growth, we are not describing a fixed pool of consumers switching between brands. We are describing a process of demand creation, where every new eye test, every new store in a Tier 2+ town, and every first-time customer discovering their need for vision correction expands the market itself.This demand-supply gap is underpinned by a large and growing refractive error burden. In India alone, the affected population is estimated to exceed 943 million by 2030 and continues to rise, with a significant proportion remaining uncorrected due to affordability constraints, limited awareness, 
and inadequate access to optometry services. This structural disconnect between need and access reinforces the long-term opportunity for market creation.
India's macroeconomic environment in FY26 was 
mixed. While overall GDP growth remained robust at an estimated 6.3 - 6.8%, consumption patterns were uneven. Urban demand slowed, driven by sustained retail inflation which climbed to 3.87% by March 2026, and high rental inflation, leading to stress in several FMCG and retail sectors where volume growth slowed to single digits
1,2. Despite these broader 
consumption headwinds, the organised retail sector, particularly experience-led categories showed resilience, with retail growth accelerating from 4-5% at the beginning of the fiscal year to 10-11% during the festive season
3. One of the key developments 
specific to the prescription eyewear industry was the Government of India's decision to reduce the Goods and Services Tax (GST) on prescription eyeglasses and contact lenses from 12% to 5% in September 2025
4. This policy shift demonstrates 
the growing size of the problem and makes essential vision care more affordable.
The recent geopolitical developments have created 
macroeconomic uncertainties for India and the global economy at large, marked by the devaluation of the Indian Rupee against key foreign currencies, supply chain disruptions, and potential inflation. Vision correction is a recurring need that consumers cannot defer indefinitely, and the essential, medical nature of prescription eyewear provides a natural hedge against a consumption slowdown. That said, our business also has a fashion element, which may be more exposed in such a scenario. We continue to monitor demand-side dynamics carefully for indirect effects, such as the deferral of non-discretionary purchases in a prolonged inflationary environment, as well as currency-driven operational pressures that impact our import bill, logistics, and raw 
material costs.

billion eyewear market in FY26, projected to reach `2,118 billion by FY30. While each market is 
distinct in its consumer behaviour and competitive dynamics, they share a common structural thread: fragmentation, dominance by traditional opticians, rising refractive error rates, and limited disruption by D2C and organised players. Within these regions, the organised and D2C segments are outpacing overall market growth, expanding at 10-14% in Southeast Asia, 7-10% CAGR in Japan, and 15-20% in the Middle East (FY25-30). This acceleration is driven by rising value consciousness, as the high cost of prescription eyewear - often 2-3x higher than India, shifts consumers toward affordable, high-quality D2C and organised players.
Southeast Asia
Southeast Asia represents a ` 682 billion eyewear 
market in FY26 with ~65% of the population 
requiring vision correction but only ~40% wearing prescription glasses
5 - a penetration gap that 
mirrors India's opportunity. The organised eyewear market of Southeast Asia is growing at 10-14% CAGR (FY25-30).
Singapore's economy grew by 5% in 2025, 
but advance estimates for Q1 2026 showed a moderation to 4.6% growth, with the retail sector registering uneven growth
6,7. In Singapore, since the 
acquisition of Owndays, our combined market share has grown from ~10-25%.
Thailand's economic growth slowed to an estimated 
2.1% in 2025, with retail confidence dropping amid political uncertainty and slow wage growth
8. 
Despite this macro unevenness, the organised D2C segment is expanding at 10-14% CAGR. In Thailand, consumers are increasingly splitting their spending between value goods and premium brands, prioritising quality and brand reputation
9. 
This polarisation suits our dual-brand strategy - Lenskart for accessible value and Owndays for premium D2C, allowing organised players to formalise a highly fragmented market.
Japan
Japan is one of our key international opportunities 
at `787 billion (FY26). The market is undergoing a 
structural shift toward value-focused D2C brands. The D2C eyewear market of Japan is growing at 7-10% CAGR (FY25-30). Persistent retail inflation - with services inflation rising 2.6% YoY in early 2026, and declining real wages
10 have made consumers more price-sensitive. The Bank of Japan noted that 
while the economy is growing moderately, the pressure on household spending remains high
11. 
D2C market share has climbed from 25% to 31% in the last five years and is projected to reach 43% by FY30
12. This structural tailwind directly benefits our 
Owndays brand, which is positioned as the leading value-focused D2C alternative. As the third-largest D2C eyewear player with 287 stores compared to 500+ for the top two competitors, the whitespace for expansion remains substantial.
Middle East (UAE and Saudi Arabia)
The Middle East represents a ` 174 billion eyewear 
opportunity in FY26 defined by high ASPs, a young, 
digitally-native population, and strong demand for fashion-forward eyewear. The organized eyewear market of the Middle East is growing at 15-20% CAGR (FY25-30).
The UAE's real GDP expanded by 3.9% year-over-
year in early 2025, driven by a 5.3% growth in the non-hydrocarbon sector
13. In Saudi Arabia, consumer 
spending surged to SAR 1.41 trillion, fuelled by experiential retail and internet penetration exceeding 95%
14. The region is experiencing a rapid shift toward 
omnichannel retail, with e-commerce penetration in the UAE reaching 12-14% of total retail sales
15.
Our omnichannel model is a natural fit for this market. However, geopolitical tensions in the broader region have introduced supply chain uncertainties and inflationary pressures on imported premium goods
16.
2. Business Performance
FY26 validated a thesis we have been building toward for over a decade: that a vertically integrated system, where eye testing, manufacturing, supply chain, retail, technology, and brand operate as one connected platform, produces compounding returns once it reaches sufficient scale. Revenue grew 32.3% YoY to `90,023 million on a proforma basis, while EBITDA 
(pre-IndAS 116) grew at nearly twice that rate, up 96.7% to `10,091 million, expanding margins from 
7.5% to 11.2%. PAT surged 147.7% to `5,300 million.
This was not the result of cost-cutting or one-time 
tailwinds. It was the structural outcome of a system where eye tests create new customers, Gold membership converts them into recurring relationships, a widening product portfolio deepens wallet share, and technology reduces the cost of serving each incremental customer. Every layer reinforced the others in FY26. The operating and financial metrics that follow explain how.

2A. Eye Tests: The Top of the Funnel
Eye tests are the single most important leading 
indicator of our business. Every customer relationship begins with an eye test - it is the moment latent need converts into active demand. In FY26, we conducted 23.8 million eye tests globally (+48.5% YoY), with 20.7 million in India alone (+54.3%). Nearly half of all India eye tests were first-time exams, meaning we are not merely serving existing demand but creating new customers who did not previously know they needed glasses.
This growth was enabled by three 
reinforcing investments:
First, remote optometry , our AI-enabled platform 
that allows centrally located optometrists to 
conduct precise eye tests for customers hundreds of kilometres away - scaled from 168 stores at 
FY25-end to 623 stores by FY26-end in India, a 3.7x expansion in a single year. Our Centre of Excellence in Kolkata acts as a hub for this model, enabling optometrists to conduct eye tests for customers across locations with a high degree of efficiency and quality. Internationally, remote eye testing is now live in Japan and launching across Southeast Asia, bringing our total global remote optometry footprint to 908 stores. This directly unlocked Tier 2+ markets in India and underpenetrated prefectures in Japan where full-time optometrists are scarce.
Second, we enabled eye tests for children aged 
8+ across all India stores, powered by proprietary 
technology that validates multiple prescriptions and applies child-specific modifications, helping us identify vision correction needs earlier and expanding the addressable population.
=== page 157 ===
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
141Third, our store expansion itself, 603 net new 
stores globally (542 India, 61 international) brought 
eye-testing infrastructure physically closer to millions of potential customers in underpenetrated markets across geographies.
The financial logic is direct: more eye tests → more 
first-time customers → more volume → more revenue. Eye tests are the upstream driver that explains the 24.7% growth in eyewear units sold and the 22.6% growth in transacting customer accounts.
2B. Same-Store Growth and the Customer 
Franchise
Once a customer enters the system through an 
eye test, our model is designed to deepen that relationship over time. The clearest evidence that this is working is same-store sales growth - both in India and international markets.
In India, we delivered 20.8% SSSG in FY26. 
More importantly, Same-Pincode Sales Growth (SPSG) ran at 27.3%, a full 645 basis points above SSSG. This gap is a critical signal: it confirms that new stores in the same micro-market are creating incremental demand rather than cannibalising existing stores. Each additional store improves proximity, convenience, and trust - and the entire pincode grows.
Internationally, the same dynamic is playing out. 
With only 61 net new stores added in FY26, the majority of international revenue growth of 30.2% was same-store-driven. In Singapore, the dual-brand strategy (Owndays for premium, Lenskart for accessibility) is deepening wallet share within existing catchments. Japan continues to deliver strong same-store growth with improving unit economics.
One of the key engines behind this same-store 
compounding is the customer franchise we are building through Gold membership. Active Gold members in India reached 8.8 million (+29.5% YoY), generating `1,995 million in subscription fees 
(+84.7%). Compared to the India industry average of 1.8 eyeglasses over a two-year period, customer accounts acquired in our FY23 cohort achieved double the volume at 3.6 eyeglasses. Driving this impressive growth is our Gold membership programme, where members purchase at a meaningfully higher frequency. This repeat behaviour is the core of our compounding model: it generates revenue without incremental acquisition cost and deepens wallet share as customers move across frames, lenses, sunglasses, and contact lenses over time. Internationally, we have introduced the Gold membership model in Singapore and are evaluating its extension to other markets.India ASP grew 6.3% YoY to ` 1,827, reflecting 
continued premiumisation as customers choose better design, stronger lens features, and more occasion-led products. Our International segment, where ASP runs at approximately 3x India levels, benefited from the ` depreciating against the 
respective local currencies. The segment grew 20% YoY on a constant-currency basis, while ASP remained stable, on a constant currency basis, over the same period.
2C. New Store Expansion
In FY26, we added 603 net new stores globally - 542 in India (nearly double FY25’s 282) and 61 internationally, taking our total active store count to 3,327 across 16 countries. We entered 157 new cities in India, expanding our presence to 556 cities.
India
This expansion was guided by two signals: demand 
remains underpenetrated even in established markets, and the Tier 2+ opportunity is structurally deeper than anticipated. Tier 2+ markets accounted for 254 of the 542 net new stores (nearly 3x FY25’s 89) - markets where organised eyewear retail is nascent and a Lenskart store creates demand rather than competing for it. Our early Tier 2+ cohorts have shown a high share of first-time eyewear buyers, robust revenue per store, and payback under 12 months. Towns like Saharsa in Bihar, Shahdol in Madhya Pradesh, Golaghat in Assam, and Jhargram in West Bengal each delivered ~` 16-17 lakhs per 
month in revenue, confirming that the deeper we go, the larger the underserved market we find.
Our GeoIQ platform which analyses over 3,000 
variables including satellite imagery, mobility patterns, localised economic data, and a cannibalisation model made every store-opening decision data-driven. The cannibalisation model was materially strengthened in FY26, enabling us to densify aggressively while sustaining strong same store growth. GeoIQ analysis identifies potential for approximately 4,500 additional store locations in India, of which roughly 3,000 are in Tier 2+ markets, confirming that we are still in the early stages of our India expansion. India has approximately 60 optical stores per million people versus over 1,200 jewellery stores per million - the structural whitespace remains vast.
As we scale, we are increasing focus on CoCo 
(Company Owned, Company Operated) execution, particularly where greater control over premium feel, service consistency, brand presentation, and customer experience is important. Operating cash flow largely funded the accelerated store rollout.

142International
We added 61 net new stores internationally, taking our 
international active store count to 718. The pace was deliberately measured - the majority of international revenue growth was same-store-driven. Each market operates at a different lifecycle stage: Singapore is established with market leadership; Japan is scaling with improving unit economics and whitespace in underpenetrated prefectures identified by GeoIQ; Thailand is in growth mode with the Lenskart brand introduction alongside Owndays; and Saudi Arabia is in its investment phase, building the platform for future growth. In the Middle East, we operate 41 stores with revenue doubling over the last two years.
2D. Merchandising, Product Mix, and 
Premiumisation
We operate a House of Brands - each serving a 
distinct customer cohort, price point, and occasion - on a shared integrated platform. This architecture allows us to serve the full spectrum of eyewear demand across geographies: from first-time buyers seeking affordable eyewear, well-designed frames to premium customers seeking design-forward, technology-led products.
Our brand and sub-brand portfolio includes Lenskart 
AIR (comfort-led), Vincent Chase and Hustlr (value and first-time buyer), John Jacobs, Owndays, LPL, and Meller (premium and design-led), Hooper (kids), and Aqualens (contact lenses). Across these brands, our 100+ member in-house design and merchandising team launched 100+ new collections globally during FY26, translating real-time consumer insights into innovative styles using advanced computer-aided design.
We engineer precise geometries to ensure optimal 
fit across diverse facial profiles, driving functional innovations like “Turban Fit,” ultra-flexible “Twyst” hinges, and the durable “Creatr” kids’ range. Simultaneously, we tailor fashion aesthetics to regional tastes - from minimalist styles in Singapore to premium Celestia, Gilded, and Luxury Sun Edit collections in the Middle East, and fashion-forward Pop Mart collaboration in Thailand. This multiplicity, empowering consumers to own multiple pairs for different outfits, occasions, and needs is a key driver of purchase frequency across all our markets.
Product collaborations deepened cultural relevance 
across consumer cohorts globally. Partnerships with Pop Mart, Stranger Things, Harry Potter, Sanrio (Hello Kitty), and Disney drove strong engagement among younger audiences. Owndays’ partnership with DITA Lancier, one of the most respected luxury eyewear houses globally, continues to anchor our premium positioning internationally. These collaborations signal that Lenskart is present where consumers spend attention: culture, collectibles, and self-expression.
Premiumisation is accelerating. The share of India 
revenue from orders above ` 10,000 grew to 20.5%. 
In FY26, driven by higher adoption of premium frames, progressive lenses, advanced coatings, and branded offerings such as Owndays and Rodenstock lenses manufactured in our own facilities. This premiumisation is not forced through pricing - it is an outcome of better product, deeper trust, and a portfolio that gives customers reasons to trade up as their relationship with the category matures.
Meller, our Barcelona-based, digitally native 
sunglasses brand acquired in FY25 is now available across 1,000+ Lenskart stores in India and all Middle East stores, with dedicated brand stores opening. International sunglasses volumes grew 36.3% YoY, filling a historical white space in our portfolio. Meller demonstrates our ability to identify, acquire, and scale brand assets globally on the Lenskart platform - a playbook we intend to repeat.
Contact lenses represent an adjacent growth vector 
with high repeat frequency. Quick-commerce delivery for contact lenses is live in Singapore (two-hour delivery), and we are expanding same-day and next-day delivery for contacts domestically. The category benefits from convenience-driven purchasing behaviour that aligns naturally with our omnichannel infrastructure.
2E. Online and Omnichannel
Lenskart is an omnichannel platform, and the strength of that platform is increasingly evident in the numbers. ~50% of FY26 India revenue was digitally influenced (up from ~45% in FY25) - a number that reflects not just online purchases, but the full arc of omnichannel customer behaviour: customers who discover, compare, or consult digitally and then complete their purchase in-store, and equally, in-store customers who return to buy their next pair on the app. Digital is not a separate channel - it is the demand-generation layer that makes our store network more productive.
Our App
Our app has crossed 120 million cumulative 
downloads in India (up from 101 million in FY25). Unlike many commerce apps, the Lenskart app is not merely a catalogue. In eyewear, customers need confidence in fit, prescription, style, price, and service before they purchase. The app supports this journey through virtual try-on, frame measurement, AI-led recommendations powered by face-scan technology), customer reviews, appointment 
=== page 159 ===
Corporate Overview Statutory Reports Financial Statements
143booking, eye-test records, store location, order 
tracking, and repeat engagement. We are building the digital platform for global markets with local language support, such as Arabic and Thai, regional payment options, and market-specific online journeys that build trust across geographies while retaining the strength of one integrated platform.
In-Store Operations
We are systematically moving towards a 
self-service model in our stores, reducing wait times, improving throughput, and elevating the customer experience. Face-recognition-based self-check-in is now live. Self-checkout for contact lenses is live in select international markets. AI-based frame recommendation is active in-store, providing personalised suggestions based on face shape and prescription history. We have also introduced a store pick-up facility for online orders, and digitised planograms now provide real-time visibility into in-store merchandising.
Digitally influenced demand transforms our unit 
economics by boosting store productivity beyond basic foot traffic, scaling online revenue efficiently, and using our app to anchor Gold-led repeat behaviour. This ecosystem directly materialised in our financial results, unlocking same store sales growth.
Home Try-on (HTO)
For customers who cannot visit a store, whether 
elderly, mobility-constrained, or simply preferring the convenience of home - our HTO service brings the store to them. A vision care professional visits the customer at home, brings a curated set of frames, performs a 12-step eye check, and helps the customer choose and order. In FY26, HTO operated across 1,000+ pin codes, with conversion rates meaningfully above walk-in or purely digital rates and NPS higher than the overall India average.

In FY26, we made significant strides in deploying AI across both market creation and cost reduction, with a direct and measurable impact on the customer experience. At the core of this performance lies a deeply integrated technology ecosystem that connects every stage of the customer journey — where every eye test, every face scan, every transaction, and every delivery feeds into a learning loop that compounds with scale.Creating More Market

2G. Manufacturing and Supply Chain
Our manufacturing and supply chain infrastructure is the structural backbone that protects margins, enables speed, and supports premiumisation, across both India and international markets. In FY26, this infrastructure scaled meaningfully.
Prescription eyeglasses manufacturing demands 
extreme optical precision, from sub-micron computer-guided surfacing to the application of specialised protective coatings. Our fully automated lens manufacturing line operates with limited human intervention, ensuring uncompromising quality control while keeping total costs significantly below the industry average. Frame manufacturing, which began through a joint venture in China in 2017, has been progressively brought in India with mould design and manufacturing capabilities at our Bhiwadi facility.
